a good finding looks like: A personalisation tag was left unclosed and will reach subscribers as raw code where their name should be. Unambiguous, embarrassing, and invisible in every preview a creator would think to run.
a bad finding looks like: Firing on a stray brace inside ordinary copy, or inside a code sample the creator is deliberately showing. Both read as us not understanding their writing.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Tighten what counts as a tag opening before touching severity.

a good finding looks like: A conditional block was opened and never closed, so a section may vanish or render raw depending on the sending engine.
a bad finding looks like: Firing on a block closed by a variant spelling we do not recognise. The creator sees a correct email being called broken.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Widen the recognised closing forms.

a good finding looks like: A link returns an error. Anyone who clicks reaches a dead end and the email cannot be recalled to fix it.
a bad finding looks like: Firing on a site that blocks automated requests, is briefly down, or sits behind a login. The link is fine and we called it dead - the fastest way to lose a creator's trust in every other finding.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Treat request-blocking responses as unknown rather than broken.

a good finding looks like: A button or link has no destination. Readers click it and nothing happens, which wastes the one action the email was asking for.
a bad finding looks like: Firing on an anchor used purely for layout, or one the editor has not finished writing while the creator is mid-edit.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Ignore anchors with no visible text.

a good finding looks like: Body copy a reader has to work to read - on a phone, in sunlight, at the end of the day. The creator chose a colour without seeing it in those conditions.
a bad finding looks like: Firing on decorative or intentionally quiet text: a caption, a legal line, a watermark. Technically below the threshold, deliberately so, and telling the creator their design is broken when it is not.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Exempt small print by role before loosening the ratio.

a good finding looks like: A quiet note that a design already clearing the readable bar could go further. Never blocks, never insists.
a bad finding looks like: Appearing often enough to feel like nagging. This check earns its place only while creators ignore it without irritation.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Stop reporting it at all if it accounts for most ignores.

a good finding looks like: Text pinned to a colour with nothing painting behind it, so a client forcing dark mode renders it invisible. Roughly half the audience sees a blank space and the creator never finds out.
a bad finding looks like: Firing on text that would survive the repaint anyway, or on a template whose background is set somewhere we did not look. A creator seeing a correct email flagged learns to skip the whole panel.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Widen where we look for a painted surface before changing tier.

a good finding looks like: A dark-mode rule recolours text without recolouring what it sits on, so the creator's own dark styling produces unreadable output.
a bad finding looks like: Firing where the surface is painted by a rule we did not resolve. Same cost as above and harder to explain.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Improve surface resolution inside media rules.

a good finding looks like: An image carrying meaning has no description, so it is silent to anyone using a screen reader and a blank gap wherever images are blocked - which is most inboxes, by default.
a bad finding looks like: Firing on spacers, dividers and tracking pixels. Nothing is lost when those are silent, and asking a creator to describe a one-pixel image makes the whole check look mechanical.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Exclude images below a size threshold and known spacer patterns.

a good finding looks like: The description is the filename, which tells a reader nothing and usually means it was filled in automatically.
a bad finding looks like: Firing on a description that legitimately resembles a filename.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Require stronger filename evidence.

a good finding looks like: An address written out but not clickable, so readers have to copy it by hand.
a bad finding looks like: Firing where the address is shown deliberately - a domain the creator is naming rather than linking.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Skip addresses inside quotes or code.

a good finding looks like: Link text carrying none of the promise - 'click here' beside a sentence doing all the work. Costs the click, and reads as nothing to anyone moving link to link.
a bad finding looks like: Firing on short link text that is clear in context. This is a judgment call and the check should stay advisory for exactly that reason.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Shrink the phrase list to the least defensible cases.

a good finding looks like: The point of the subject line falls past where a phone truncates, so the part that earns the open is never seen.
a bad finding looks like: Firing on a subject whose point lands early and simply runs long. The length is not the problem; where the meaning sits is.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Judge where the meaning falls, not the character count.

a good finding looks like: No preview text, so the inbox fills that space with whatever the email starts with - often an unsubscribe line.
a bad finding looks like: Firing where the template supplies preview text somewhere we do not read it.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Detect template-supplied preview text.

a good finding looks like: Dense linking with little writing between, which filters read as promotional. The subscriber may never see the email at all.
a bad finding looks like: Firing on a genuine link roundup, which is a legitimate and common newsletter format. The creator knows what they are doing.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Recognise roundup formats before adjusting the ratio.

a good finding looks like: Mostly pictures with almost no writing - a spam signature, and empty for anyone whose client blocks images.
a bad finding looks like: Firing on a deliberately visual send from a creator whose whole format is imagery.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Account for alt text as copy before adjusting the threshold.

a good finding looks like: The primary action sits below where a skimming reader stops, after copy they have to wade through. The offer is in the email; most of the list never sees it.
a bad finding looks like: Firing on a long-form essay where the ask belongs at the end, or on a letter with no action in it at all. Both read as us not understanding what they write.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Raise the fold estimate before touching the check. Most disputes are about where we think the fold is, not whether a buried CTA matters.

a good finding looks like: The main action does not read as something to press - buried in a sentence, styled like body copy, or competing with three other links of equal weight.
a bad finding looks like: Firing on a deliberately quiet, text-first newsletter. A creator whose whole voice is understated is being told to shout.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Retire it before recalibrating. Prominence is taste, and a taste check that creators disagree with has no defensible threshold to move to.

a good finding looks like: Phrasing filters are known to weight, in a send that gained nothing from it - an unnecessary risk on mail that cannot be recalled.
a bad finding looks like: Firing on the creator's actual subject matter. A newsletter about discounts will say 'free', and flagging that is us mistaking their topic for a defect.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Weight the phrase against the topic before dropping it. This check should read the send, not a word list.

a good finding looks like: A reader has to work to find what they are being asked to do - the ask is buried in qualification, or three asks compete in one paragraph.
a bad finding looks like: Firing on style. Long sentences, digression and a slow build are choices, and flagging them is the closest this product ever comes to editing someone's voice.
first lever if creators say it is wrong: Retire it. Of every check here this is the one most likely to be us having an opinion about writing, which is not what we are for.
